content:
If your air cargo has landed in Jeddah or Madinah, check when the cargo terminal can hand it over before sending a truck. Freight forwarders on the ground report cargo backlogs at both airports. Their estimate is 6–7 days for customs clearance in Jeddah, with some shipments taking longer, and 4–5 days in Madinah. These are estimates from field reports. For your own shipment, ask for the number of pieces the terminal has received, the latest customs status and the expected pickup date. If your consignment was split across flights, ask for those details for each batch.

What forwarders are seeing in Jeddah and Madinah

The clip above was filmed at the Jeddah airport cargo terminal around November 13. Rows of air cargo pallets and containers can be seen in the outdoor handling area.

AIDUK's field update says part of the cargo originally due to arrive via Riyadh or Dammam was redirected to Jeddah. Forwarders report tight storage and handling space at Jeddah, where the terminal is prioritizing cargo already in the backlog. The same update reports congestion at Madinah, where limited warehouse space is under pressure from higher volumes.

The forwarder update gives the following clearance estimates. It does not specify when the count starts or whether it uses calendar or working days. If you need to set a delivery date, ask your forwarder for the latest estimate against your air waybill and the time the terminal expects to make the cargo available.

Arrival airportClearance estimate from field reports
Jeddah (JED)6–7 days. Some shipments may take longer.
Madinah (MED)4–5 days. Timing depends on the terminal’s progress.

Your flight has landed. Where are the cartons?

A flight arrival can show up before the cargo has been unloaded, taken to the terminal or scanned into the warehouse. In some cases the warehouse has the goods and the customs record is still pending or being matched to the air waybill. Ask your forwarder for a piece count and the last confirmed event. That gives your receiving team something it can actually schedule around.

  1. Terminal receipt. How many pieces have been physically received and scanned in? Ask what is still awaiting unloading, sorting or transfer.
  2. Customs clearance. Has the declaration been submitted? Ask whether the shipment is awaiting inspection or has already been released.
  3. Pickup. Has the terminal confirmed that the cargo is available for collection? Use its pickup window to book the truck and the receiving slot at your warehouse.

If the airline's tracking page and the broker's update show different statuses, first confirm that both refer to the same air waybill and batch. Then ask for the timestamp of the latest terminal or customs update.

If your shipment was split across flights

Ask the forwarder for a breakdown by flight or batch: pieces booked, pieces received, and pieces released and ready for pickup. One batch can show as received while the remainder is still waiting to be unloaded or scanned. If your delivery depends on a complete set, such as a machine and its installation parts, check that the full set is available before booking the truck. If partial pickup would help, ask the terminal or forwarder whether it can release and hand over that batch separately.

Before you book urgent air cargo from China

Give the forwarder the latest date you can receive the cargo at your warehouse. Ask for two dates in return: the estimated flight arrival and the estimated pickup date. If the booking may be split, ask whether the pieces that must arrive together can travel in one batch. If an alternative arrival airport is proposed, check where customs clearance will take place and how the cargo will reach your final delivery address.

Send DDNZ your shipment details. For freight already booked, include the air waybill, piece count and latest status. For a new booking, send the China pickup point, cargo dimensions and weight, delivery city and required receiving date.
